GEO-MIQUEL-01.remember: For D,E,F on the side-lines of triangle ABC, circles (AEF), (BFD), (CDE) pass through one common Miquel point.
GEO-MIQUEL-01.link: The executable proof is “two circles first”: define M as their second intersection, then prove M lies on the third.
GEO-MIQUEL-01.why: Cyclicity rewrites angles at M as angles at the original triangle vertices; the rewritten angles combine to satisfy the third cyclic test.
GEO-MIQUEL-01.notice: Three circles each using one triangle vertex and the two adjacent side-points.
GEO-MIQUEL-01.try: Choose M from the first two circles. Do not invoke the theorem name as a magic step.
GEO-MIQUEL-01.contrast: Keep side-extension orientation consistent when using directed angles.
GEO-MIQUEL-01.example: If M lies on (AEF) and (BFD), rewrite ∠EMF and ∠FMD using the corresponding vertex angles, then test C,D,E,M for cyclicity.

GEO-TANGENT-01.remember: Radius to a tangent point is perpendicular to the tangent. Tangents from the same external point to the same circle are equal. The line of centres is perpendicular to a common chord.
GEO-TANGENT-01.link: A tangent should trigger a right angle before any long angle chase.
GEO-TANGENT-01.why: The radius to the closest point of a tangent line is perpendicular; equal tangent lengths follow from congruent right triangles.
GEO-TANGENT-01.notice: “Tangent at T”, two tangents from one point, or two intersecting circles with a common chord.
GEO-TANGENT-01.try: Draw the radius to each contact point immediately.
GEO-TANGENT-01.contrast: Equal tangents must come from one external point to one circle.
GEO-TANGENT-01.example: If PA and PB are tangents from P to one circle, then PA=PB.

GEO-CIRCLEPACK-01.remember: Two externally tangent circles of radii r1,r2 touching the same line have horizontal centre separation d=2√(r1r2). Tangent circles are related by homothety at the tangency point.
GEO-CIRCLEPACK-01.link: Circle packing becomes one-dimensional after projecting the centres to the common tangent line.
GEO-CIRCLEPACK-01.why: The centre distance is r1+r2 and the vertical difference is |r1-r2|; Pythagoras gives d²=(r1+r2)²-(r1-r2)²=4r1r2.
GEO-CIRCLEPACK-01.notice: Multiple circles tangent to one baseline or internally/externally tangent at a shared point.
GEO-CIRCLEPACK-01.try: Drop perpendicular radii to the common tangent and write centre gaps.
GEO-CIRCLEPACK-01.contrast: Identify internal versus external tangency before using a centre-distance formula.
GEO-CIRCLEPACK-01.example: Radii 9 and 4 on one tangent line have horizontal centre gap 2√36=12.

GEO-TRIG-01.remember: sin=opposite/hypotenuse, cos=adjacent/hypotenuse, tan=opposite/adjacent; a/sin A=b/sin B=c/sin C=2R; c²=a²+b²-2ab cos C.
GEO-TRIG-01.link: Trig is a geometry tool, not a default. Use it when side-angle data is more direct than a synthetic theorem.
GEO-TRIG-01.why: Sine/cosine rules extend right-triangle ratios to arbitrary triangles; the sine-area formula links angles to area.
GEO-TRIG-01.notice: Known opposite side-angle pair -> sine rule; two sides + included angle or all three sides -> cosine rule.
GEO-TRIG-01.try: Write the side opposite each named angle before choosing a formula.
GEO-TRIG-01.contrast: Do not use trig when one circle/similarity theorem already closes the problem.
GEO-TRIG-01.example: If A=30°, B=45°, a=6, then b=6·sin45°/sin30° and b²=72.

GEO-COORD-01.remember: Choose coordinates to make the strongest structure automatic. Distance²=(x2-x1)²+(y2-y1)²; midpoint averages coordinates; perpendicular vectors have dot product 0.
GEO-COORD-01.link: Coordinates are especially effective for rectangles, symmetric triangles, circles with known centres, and many perpendicularities.
GEO-COORD-01.why: A good placement turns geometric constraints into zero coordinates, equal coordinates, or simple linear equations.
GEO-COORD-01.notice: Many numeric perpendicularities, axis-aligned rectangles, arc intersections, or symmetry.
GEO-COORD-01.try: Place the longest/most constrained line on an axis before assigning unknown coordinates.
GEO-COORD-01.contrast: Bad coordinates add variables. Use them only if they reduce the work.
GEO-COORD-01.example: For an isosceles triangle, placing the base endpoints at (-a,0),(a,0) puts the apex on x=0 automatically.

GEO-VECTOR-01.remember: Midpoint M=(A+B)/2, centroid G=(A+B+C)/3. For consecutive parallelogram A,B,C,D: D=A+C-B.
GEO-VECTOR-01.link: Vectors are excellent for repeated parallelograms and centroid identities because midpoint/centroid operations are linear.
GEO-VECTOR-01.why: Parallelogram completion and centroid averaging are affine operations, so the coordinate-free vector equations stay short.
GEO-VECTOR-01.notice: Repeated parallelograms, centroids, or a sum of squared distances from a centre point.
GEO-VECTOR-01.try: Choose an origin that makes one important point zero - often the centroid or an arbitrary common point O.
GEO-VECTOR-01.contrast: Do not expand coordinates component-by-component if a single vector identity works.
GEO-VECTOR-01.example: If O is the origin and OAEB is a parallelogram, then e=a+b.

GEO-LOCUS-01.remember: Equidistant from two points -> perpendicular bisector. Equidistant from two intersecting lines -> two angle bisectors. Fixed distance from a point -> circle. Fixed distance from a line -> two parallels.
GEO-LOCUS-01.link: Construction problems become easier when the target condition is first translated into a locus or a ratio.
GEO-LOCUS-01.why: Each locus is exactly the set of points satisfying the distance condition, so an intersection of loci solves simultaneous constraints.
GEO-LOCUS-01.try: State the locus in words before drawing compass arcs or parallels.
GEO-LOCUS-01.contrast: Check edge cases: if a given line coincides with an angle-bisector locus, there can be infinitely many points.
GEO-LOCUS-01.example: A point equidistant from A and B must lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

GEO-OPT-01.remember: For fixed base, triangle area is maximized by maximizing perpendicular height. For a fixed chord in a fixed circle, the farthest point from the chord-line lies on the perpendicular diameter.
GEO-OPT-01.link: Optimization is usually about the variable inside the target formula, not the visually longest segment.
GEO-OPT-01.why: With base fixed, area=(1/2)bh is linear in height, so the geometry reduces to a farthest-point problem.
GEO-OPT-01.notice: “Maximum area”, fixed base/chord, or a shape constrained to a circle.
GEO-OPT-01.try: Write the target formula and identify the only variable quantity.
GEO-OPT-01.contrast: Do not optimize a side length merely because it changes in the picture.
GEO-OPT-01.example: Among triangles with base 10, height 8 has larger area than height 6 regardless of the slanted sides.

GEO-MENS-01.remember: Cube side s: edge s, face diagonal s√2, body diagonal s√3, surface area 6s², volume s³. Closed cylinder: TSA=2πr(r+h), V=πr²h.
GEO-MENS-01.link: Mensuration questions often add an integer or interpretation filter after the formula.
GEO-MENS-01.why: The main difficulty is usually identifying which geometric distance or surface the coordinates/formula represent.
GEO-MENS-01.notice: 3D coordinates, cube vertex distances, cylinder surface/volume relations.
GEO-MENS-01.try: Classify a cube segment as edge, face diagonal, or body diagonal before solving for s.
GEO-MENS-01.contrast: Do not assume two coordinate differences show an edge; an edge changes only one coordinate in an axis-aligned model.
GEO-MENS-01.example: A cube body diagonal d gives s=d/√3 and surface area 6s².
